title: A Measure-Theoretic Analysis of Reasoning in Transformers: Structural Generalization and Approximation Limits
claim: Added model capacity helps only up to a ceiling, and absolute positional encoding collapses at scale while relative encoding stays stable.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; line and scatter plots; red vs blue colors
description: A 2x2 grid of four plots comparing absolute positional encoding (red) with rotary encoding (blue). Panel A is a scatter of accuracy against layer depth. Markers show the training distribution, and a dashed black curve marks the theoretical ceiling that every point stays under. Panel B plots accuracy against parameter count for Balanced, Wide and Deep models. The red Wide line (dashed with square markers) falls steeply at 300M parameters while the blue lines stay flat or rise. Panel C shows Wide models on a mixed distribution. Red drops sharply to a dotted red line labeled as Omega(1) representation collapse, while blue keeps rising. Panel D is a slope chart of BFS-trained models across the BFS, MIXED and DFS evaluation sets. Most blue lines sit above the red ones. The red collapse curves draw the eye first.
caption: Validation of capacity bounds. (A) Supremum capacity limit on µDF S: all accuracies lie below the calibrated upper bound curve (Appendix G.3). (B) Scaling limits: width plateaus and, under APE, collapses at Large scale (Wide 0.4835 vs. Deep 0.5115); with RoPE, Wide matches Deep. (C) Sequence equivariance on µMIXED, where scaling Wide APE architectures triggers representation collapse, which RoPE prevents. (D) All BFS-trained models on the three evaluation sets, ordered by Wasserstein distance from νBF S; RoPE outperforms APE on average on each set (in 23 of 27 comparisons). The sets share one problem distribution, so the decline toward µDF S reflects the difficulty of their problem samples (Appendix K.5).
abstract: Scaling laws for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) are well documented, but little theory explains their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. We formalize reasoning with optimal transport: each search trajectory is mapped to twelve structural coordinates, such as tree depth and backtracking rate, and dataset shift is measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance. Kantorovich duality bounds the OOD risk through this distance, the architecture's Lipschitz constant and approximation limits. First, under absolute positional encoding (APE), shifting part of a trajectory to later positions almost surely changes the attention scores within that part; if this misroutes exact-match search, the Lipschitz constant and risk are $Î©(1)$. Shift-invariant encodings such as rotary position embedding (RoPE) leave the scores unchanged and bound the error. Second, we map backtracking to a Dyck-$k$ language and, under an implicit-depth assumption, derive a risk floor for search trees deeper than a multiple of the number of layers. Enough layers remove this floor; more width only shrinks a separate Barron-space approximation term. Experiments with 54 trained Transformers on combinatorial search (Countdown) support these bounds. Appendix experiments measure structural shifts in public agent, embodied and robot trajectories, shift all position indices of 33 public language models, and split deeply nested tasks into separate model calls.
